subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Radio Astronomy: Invisible Signals
description: A fast breakdown of Radio Astronomy: Invisible Signals for builders.

hook.text: Karl Jansky discovered radio waves from space in 1932 while investigating telephone static for Bell Labs.

buildup.text: The signal peaked every 23 hours and 56 minutes—matching a sidereal day. It came from the center of the Milky Way.

discovery.text: Grote Reber built the first radio telescope in his backyard in 1937. For years, he was the only radio astronomer alive.

twist.text: Radio astronomy revealed pulsars, quasars, and the Cosmic Microwave Background—none visible through optical telescopes.

climax.text: Today, arrays like ALMA and the VLA map the invisible universe in stunning detail.

punchline.text: Telephone static led to a new way of seeing the cosmos.

quiz.question: How was radio astronomy accidentally discovered?
options: Karl Jansky detected radio waves from space while investigating telephone static
A military radar station picked up signals from Jupiter
An amateur astronomer pointed a radio antenna at the Moon

details.summary: Radio astronomy began in 1932 when Karl Jansky accidentally detected radio waves from the Milky Way's center. This opened an invisible universe — radio telescopes discovered quasars, pulsars, the cosmic microwave background, and mapped hydrogen throughout the galaxy, revealing structures invisible…
details.whyItMatters: Radio astronomy proved the universe emits far more than visible light. Opening the radio window revealed entirely new classes of objects and phenomena, establishing multi-wavelength astronomy as essential for understanding the cosmos.
takeaways: Jansky discovered cosmic radio waves in 1932 accidentally
Radio telescopes discovered pulsars, quasars, and the CMB
They revealed an invisible universe beyond optical light

faq.question: How do radio telescopes work?
faq.answer: They use large dish antennas (or arrays of dishes) to collect radio waves from space, focusing them onto sensitive receivers. Because radio wavelengths are much longer than light, radio telescopes must be enormous for good resolution.

faq.question: What is the biggest radio telescope?
faq.answer: China's FAST (Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope), completed in 2016, with a 500-meter diameter. The former record holder was Arecibo (305 meters), which collapsed in 2020.
